messages.subject: MSstats v3.3.11 is released.
messages.body_plain:
Dear MSstats users,

MSstats v3.3.11 is released. Please check it in msstats.org <http://msstats.org>.

1. New functionalities : calculation of the LOD and LOQ

     (a) linear_quantlim  : with a linear fit

     (b) nonlinear_quantlim  : with a nonlinear fit

     (c) plot_quantlim  : plot of the curve used to calculate LOD and LOQ

     (d) Two example datasets, SpikeInDataLinear , SpikeInDataNonLinear are available.

     (e) One additional package, minpack.lm, is required.

     Please check help files for details.

2. Selecting high quality features in dataProcess  temporarily defaults to featureSubset='top3' . Updates for this option will be available in the next release.

3. Allow colon (:) in the peptide sequence. (Thanks, Eugene)

4. Fix the bug for fillIncompleteRows in dataProcess : If there are only one feature which has incomplete rows, the issue for getting run and feature ID in dataProcess and not show the list. Now, it works.

5. Change the default for ylimUp in dataProcessPlots for profile plot and QC plot. The upper limit of y-axis with ylimUp=FALSE  is calculated by maximum log2(intensity) across all proteins after normalization + 3 and then rounding off to the nearest integer. (Thanks, Andreas)

6. Fix the bug for dataProcess : When the number of proteins for xxx$ProcessedData and xxx$RunlevelData are different, the bug happened for calculating %missing and imputation. (Thanks, John)

Please let us know if you have any difficulty.

- MSstats developers

messages.subject: effect size statistics
messages.body_plain:
Dear MSstats team,

following the concepts shown in this Nature methods article

http://www.nature.com/nmeth/journal/v12/n3/full/nmeth.3288.html

I am trying to generate an effect size statistics using MSstats output. Unfortunately, I am a missing some crucial information which could be easily added to the current MSstats report, or is only a few clicks away, but the current column labels are not really precise, so I am not sure if my interpretations and calculations are correct. I created a two group comparison (let's call the exp. conditions A and B) and the MSstats report contains the following variables:

A vs. B, log2FC, SE, df, t.value, p.value and adj.p.value

What I nedd to understand is the following:

a) A vs. B is a label for the contrast I suppose. Which condition of this contrast was used as the base level in the lm(e)? A or B?
b) I assume in a 2group comparison the log2FC is my effect size estimate, correct?
c) SE is the standard error of the log2FC, meaning the std. error of my effect size estimate?
d) Which t.value is given here? How was it calculated (sig. level? 95%, one-tail? two-tails?) What is it referring to?
e) How was the p-value calculated? Is it coming from a post-hoc test? So in my case a two-sample t-test? Or was it calculated differently e.g. by simulation?

What I would like to do now is to calculate an 95% CI for my effect size estimate (log2FC). Is this formula correct?

low.95%.CI = log2FC-t.value(95%two-tailed t.value, df)*SE
high.95%.CI = log2FC+t.value(95%two-tailed t.value, df)*SE

What I realised is that the t.value given in the table is NOT the same as when I look into a t.distribution table for a two-tailed 95% t-value at df as given in the table. How come? Is there a handy way to plot effect size estimates and their 95%CIs for a large number of features (something like the vulcano plot of effect size statistics?)

Greetings,
Tobi

messages.subject_clean: TopN vs ALL and Individual vs summed ions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tobi,

A reason is that features from one run are measured together (as a block), and it's important to partition the within-run and between-run variabilities accordingly, especially if they don't share similar characteristics. MSstats implements this idea by partitioning the variability into two levels, as a subplot to make a restriction on randomization and characterize the variability within runs, followed by a whole plot to characterize the between-run variability.

Hope this helps
Tsung-Heng

Unfortunately, I am a missing some crucial information which could be easily added to the current MSstats report, or is only a few clicks away, but the current column labels are not really precise, so I am not sure if my interpretations and calculations are correct. I created a two group comparison (let's call the exp. conditions A and B) and the MSstats report contains the following variables:
>
> A vs. B, log2FC, SE, df, t.value, p.value and adj.p.value
>
> What I nedd to understand is the following:
>
> a) A vs. B is a label for the contrast I suppose. Which condition of this contrast was used as the base level in the lm(e)? A or B?

This depends on the contrast matrix you specify. For example, if you want to compare A-B, which means log(A)-log(B) and the same as log(A/B), set '1' for A and '-1' for B in the row of your contrast matrix.

> b) I assume in a 2group comparison the log2FC is my effect size estimate, correct?

Correct.

> c) SE is the standard error of the log2FC, meaning the std. error of my effect size estimate?

Correct.

> d) Which t.value is given here? How was it calculated (sig. level? 95%, one-tail? two-tails?) What is it referring to?

It's t-statistic: the difference between two group means (on log scale), divided by the standard error of the difference.

> e) How was the p-value calculated? Is it coming from a post-hoc test? So in my case a two-sample t-test? Or was it calculated differently e.g. by simulation?

It's calculated by comparing the test statistic against the t-distribution (two-tailed hypothesis is considered).

messages.subject: Re: effect size statistics
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tobi,

to add to Tsung-Heng's comments:

- Not sure about the problem with the tables. For example, for a two-sided test at the significance level of 0.95, you need to look for the t-value such that the area under the Student distribution to the right of this value is 1-0.05/2. If this is difficult you can use the functions in R 'qt' and 'pt'.

- Please keep in mind that in the case of multiple proteins the p-value needs to be adjusted for multiple testing (see adj.p.value), and the level of the confidence interval also needs to be adjusted for multiplicity. The paper that you cite only focuses on one test and does not address the multiplicity.

HTH
Olga

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tobi,

To add to Tsung-Heng's comments:

There is indeed a big change in MSstats 3.0 and later. This is not a change in modeling philosophy, but a natural evolution. This allows us to express the experimental designs in a more appropriate and more flexible form. As Tsung-Heng mentioned, we now distinguish the within-run and between run technical variation. This also allows us to account for missing values and for outliers. There is a substantial empirical evidence that this is a better approach. We are now finalizing a manuscript that presents both the update to the models and the experimental evaluation. Apologies for not being able to make the manuscript available sooner.

Sincerely
Olga
